parts.text:
38 Carbon-14 decays into nitrogen-14 by emitting a – particle.
Which statement explains why the – particles are emitted with a range of different kinetic
energies?
A
The carbon-14 nuclei have slightly different masses.
B
The emitted – particles have a range of different masses.
C
The energy released in the decay process is different for each carbon-14 nucleus that
decays.
D
The energy released in the decay process is shared between the nitrogen-14 nucleus, a
– particle and an antineutrino.

hints: Notice every decay is the same $^{14}$C to $^{14}$N transition, so the total energy released by the mass change is fixed for each nucleus.
Recall that $\beta^-$ decay conserves lepton number by emitting an antineutrino as well as the electron, making it a three-product decay.
Consider how a fixed total energy split in different proportions between the $\beta^-$ particle and the antineutrino would change the kinetic energy left for the $\beta^-$ particle.
walkthrough: Identify the process: a neutron in $^{14}$C changes to a proton in $^{14}$N, emitting a $\beta^-$ particle. The parent and daughter nuclides are the same in every decay.
State the energy rule: the total energy available is fixed by the mass difference, $E = \Delta m c^2$, and must be conserved among all the decay products.
Note that $\beta^-$ decay is a three-body decay: $^{14}$C $\rightarrow$ $^{14}$N + $\beta^-$ + antineutrino. The nitrogen nucleus recoil energy is very small but the remaining energy is shared.
Explain the sharing: in one decay the antineutrino may carry almost all the shared energy and the $\beta^-$ very little, while in another decay the reverse can happen, with many splits in between.
Conclude that this random sharing gives a continuous range of $\beta^-$ kinetic energies from near zero up to a maximum, rather than a single value. This is option D.

A.explanation: All carbon-14 nuclei are identical, so the mass defect and total energy released per decay is the same each time.

B.explanation: Every $\beta^-$ particle is an electron with the same rest mass, so mass variation cannot produce the continuous energy spectrum.

C.explanation: The $^{14}$C to $^{14}$N transition has a fixed disintegration energy, so a varying total energy cannot explain the range of $\beta^-$ energies.

D.explanation: The fixed decay energy is shared randomly between three products, so the $\beta^-$ particle can take any fraction up to a maximum value.
